## Chinese
### 美國遊蹤
**大頭B**
終於來到美國了,我「偷運」的牛 肉乾、蝦米、長城牌罐頭豬肉等都順利 過關,和我一起的一對老夫婦卻沒有我 那麼好運,他們所帶的豬肉乾牛肉乾都 被沒收,在夏威夷過海關要很「蠱惑」 ,因為那些海關人員也很「蠱惑」,他們識聽識講中文,當你過關時卻扮什麼 也不懂,耐心等待你露出馬腳,將你的 寶貝沒收。 
### 羅省 
我再飛數小時,便到西岸最大的城 市 Los Angeles, 美國給我的第 一個印象是大部份的房屋都很矮,高樓 大厦都集中在 Down - Town。我在 Los Angeles 只見東西錯的馬路及 天橋,就算是一個住在那裏數十年的美 國人,也有機會迷路。因為LA地方太 大,公共交通又不大方便,汽車可說得 是必需品,車輛的數目很多,上班下班 時也有嚴重的塞車問題。我在LA的數 天分別住在兩個香港旅美的朋友及一對 美國夫婦的家中。 
我的朋友是一對兄妹,哥哥在LA 做事,而妹妹在 Whittier College (NIXON 也會在這間大學讀書)。 他們的生活很簡單和平淡,甚至有些苦 問。在那裏我認識了一個中國大陸的交 換生,他已經四十來歲,在國內的大學 畢業,他到美國是讀英語的學士學位。 我和他也談過文化大革命及民主運動, 他對政治已失去信心,他不過只求三餐 溫飽、家人平安,能夠這樣,他已經很 滿足了。
我在LA遊過 Down-Town,較 熱鬧的是Broadway,有很多商店及 電影院,有點兒像香港的旺角,在這裏 可以看見很多不同類型或生活方式的人 我也可以感覺到黑人、白人及墨哥西 人都有着不同的文化,黑人的走路姿態 好像是在跳舞,有些還帶着一部錄音收 音機,邊唱邊跳,當他和你說話時,他的 但語、發音及語調都能使你完全不明白 LA大會堂前有一個 John Lennon 的銅像,時常有人擺些花朵在這銅像的 跟前,除了大會堂外,LA的 Civic Centre 也有不少面積龐大的建築物。 離開 Civic Centre 不遠的地方有 Little Tokyo及 Chinatown,分別 是日本人及中國人集中及居住的地方, 這兩處地方都有點風味,Chinatown 的街道很、房屋也頗矮,路旁都有很 多食店、錄影帶及影音公司、雜貨店及銀行。
美國的怪聞 你相信與否?美國也有社會主義 向的地方政府!在這裏的一個County (叫做 Santa Monica),一批激進 的社會主義份子在選舉中勝出,他們互 相以同志(Comrade)稱呼,將那地 方的名字改為 Peoples' Republic of Santa Monica,更推行一連串社會 改革,例如管制大企業在該區的活動及 發展。他們接受電視台訪問時也承認是 推行社會主義的政策,但聯邦及州政府 卻好像沒有施加壓力去改變他們,我也 很難想像美國政府會容許這些事情存在。
### 美國的家庭生活
我在LA會住在一對年老夫妻的房 子中,丈夫是一個退了休的空軍上校, 他現在在一所著名的太空及航空工程公 司担任 Contract Manager。第二次 世界大戰時會在四川及桂林一帶駐守, 駕駛 B-19轟炸機,他非常喜歡中國人 ,因為他的飛機在一次執行任務時被擊 落,有賴中國人的幫助,才能在數星期 內由敵方的控制範圍返回自己的基地, 他有很多珍貴的回憶一飛虎隊的隊員、 桂林的山水等,他保留了很多以前的照 片。 我和他相處,也可以感受得到美國 人很尊重個人,他會很關心別人的感覺 及需要,但不會詢問別人的過去生活及 經歷。另外一些事也反映出他很尊重別 人的Privacy,我住在他屋子下層的客 房中,他不會隨便入來客房打掃,他的 房間在屋子上層,他也沒有請我參觀。 他曾說過:「Maturity is know ing how to live with unresolved conflicts.」,他今年六十二歲了,還 在UCLA的Extension Centre 選修 一些人事管理的學科,又要參加考試。 我不知道戰爭對他的影響有多大,他也 曾參加策劃越戰的工作。他是一個軍人 ,卻沒有我想像中軍人的性格或脾氣。 在家庭生活中,他也分担一切的家務, 從他和他妻子的關係,我也知道到他不 是大男人主義者。 美國的老人家大都很喜歡寵物,他 「們也不例外,他們的兒女都不在他們的 身邊,感情沒有寄托,只好養着三數隻 狗,像對待親生兒女那般地對待這些狗 隻,它們是這對夫婦生活的一部份,可 能世界就是這樣的不公平,這些寵物的 食住都比很多黑人及墨西哥人為佳。
### Arizona
我在 Arizona 的 Phoenix 逗留 了五天,參加一些當地的旅行團,遊覽 Grand Canyon & Tucson) Grand Canyon 是世界七大奇景之一。站在峽 谷的邊緣,可以看見七千餘呎下之河道 也可以看見相隔數哩的另一邊。因為 太陽的光線及雲的投影,大峽谷一層一 層的沉積岩,都顯出幾種獨特的顏色。 這個峽谷的宏偉氣氛使人感到自己在自 然界中的渺少,甚至使人恐懼。大峽谷 好像一座莊嚴、神聖的宮殿默默地在歷 史中演化。
Tucson 有着濃厚的西部氣息,最 令人難忘的卻是仙人掌,我在前往Old Town Tucson途中,都可以看到無數 幾十呎高的仙人掌,活像一個綠色的巨 人,聳立在廣潤的沙漠中。Old Town Tucson是一處片場,以前用來拍攝西 部電影,現在卻變為遊客中心,每天 都有警匪槍戰上演,還有很多模仿十 八九世紀西部小鎮的建築物,這裏也有 唐人街,當時的華人大都是礦工或鐵路 工人,也有些華人辦洗衣店賺錢過活。 Tucson附近的 St. Xavior Mission ,是一座歷史悠久的教堂,很有西班牙 的風味。在這些地方,我也會幻想自己是一個西部的拓荒者，到處探險及發掘新  奇及刺激的事物·在Tucson 的 Desert  Zoo，養着很多活的蜘蛛、蠍子、蜈蚣  、蛇及其它沙漠的動物，当我看到這些  動物時，不禁想起我的朋友曾說：「在  Arizona生活真不易，温度太高，而  且家里時常出現那些可以奪命的黑寡婦  ！他結果從Arizona的Mesa搬到  California的Sunnyvale。  
我在Phoenix期間住在YMCA，  我還隱約記得我在那里第一次嗅到大麻  ——一陣陣撲鼻的焦味。Phoenix的  氣溫很高（大約是華氏一百一十度），  而且濕度很低，很容易中暑。在星期六  星期日，Phoenix整個城好像是個鬼  城，只有很少人在街中徘徊，大部份的  店舖都不营業，公共巴士也停駛。街上 遊荡的大多是醉汉、黑人和墨西哥人，  他們多是非常貧窮。我數次在超級市場  買食物填肚時看見一些黑人不夠錢買食  用品的尷尬境况，他们大都是想用盡身  上的錢買最多的東西，例如他們身上有  七元二角，他們會想買總值七元三角的  貨品，希望收銀員不計較，他們通常都  不成功，接着他們會和收銀員理論一番，實行拖延政策，收銀員的態度强硬，  他們知道不能施其技，便會放棄一件貨 品。 
我還記起一天晚上，我和一個法國 游客返回YMCA途中碰见一个年青的  黑人，他拿着一個小牌子問我们刻在牌 子上面的文字，他並不識字，（牌上有  God Grant You Serenity)我讀給他聽，他不明白Grant 及 Serenity  的解釋。墨西哥人的命運也頗悲慘，他們大多是非法移民，收入低微，我在 Phoenix曾到過一些貧民區，雖然環 境不像香港那麽惡劣，但大部份的房屋  都很破舊，後園堆满了損壞的傢具及車  輛。  
我在Phoenix認識的波蘭裔法國 游客是一個典型的法國人，他留着很有  型的八字鬚，為人很浪漫，喜歡浪跡天  涯，雖然他已是一個三十二歲的中學教  員，但也保持着一些「童真」。當他和  我到State Capital 的附近游覽時，  恰好自動澆水系統開動供水給周圍的草  地及植物，他立刻将鞋子脱掉，跑到草  去玩水，大叫「Oh！Yo！Yo！Yo！」  
在短短兩三天的相處過程中，我學 會了很多關於美國在歐洲的文化背景，  我這位法國朋友遊歷過歐陸大部份的地 方，到過美國九次。最令我印象深刻的  是他回到波蘭旅行的經驗，在波蘭有很  多荒謬的事情發生，例如旅館的租金分為三等，最昂貴的是給來自資本主義國  家的游客，接着是友好國家（包括波蘭  本身的人民）的旅客，而價錢最特惠的是給蘇聯人。  
### SAN FRANCISCO 
San Franciso是一個很奇怪但  很有特色的城市，有着各種各類的人一  gays and lesbians tourists, drug-pushers, radicals, all kinds of  religious fanatics，龍蛇混集，但  San Francisco 給人的感覺是愉快、輕鬆及友善的·Golden Gate Bridge，  
Fisherman's Wharf 及 Golden Gate Park都是好去處，還有Cable Cars, Chinatown及All Kinds of  Entertainment (You Know What  I Mean!)  在San Francisco的色情事業很  
發達，有很多 XXX-Rated Movies  、真人表演，這些真人表演是名符其實  的真人表演，因為表演女郎可能邀請顧  客上台和她作示範演出「打真軍」。單  是X Rated Movies，已經有很多的 大胆鏡頭，只要是想像得到的都可以在  銀幕上見到·這些X-Rated Movies  ，看上十五二十分鐘便没有趣味了，根  本毫無神秘感可言，看得多倒會反胃。  
美国的香港學生  我有朋友住在Sunnywale，他一  面在 Stanford 讀 Engineering，一  
面在一間大規模的電子廠做工作，收入也算可觀，  每月有二千元美金。他住的apartment 有四五百呎實用面積，租金大約是四百元。他在美國的生  活頗沉問，放假時只好和朋友到一些 National Parks露营或旅行。我和他也到過 King's Canyon 及 Sequoia National Park旅行，看過一些大松  树及世界上最大的树（General  Sherman Tree），這些松树在阳光底下兌現特別的紅色，而且有些樹的形  狀很奇特，松子的體積很大，有些長度達八至十吋，直徑也有兩三吋。 
我在 Oregon 也探望了一位朋友，他在 University of Oregon，  Eugene讀Ph.D.，他在大學中做TA，生活休悠，我和他到過海邊的一個小鎮Florenceo那處有一個 Sand Dune  ，長四十餘哩、闊兩三哩，若要到海邊  ，便要經過這個像沙漠的 Sand Dune  ，我們也嘗試了在這「沙漠」步行的滋  味，我們結果花了差不多二小時才到海  邊，那里差不多沒有人，沙灘上有一陣  一陣的薄霧，被清凉的海風吹散。海水很凍，只有幾羣海鳥在水邊徘徊。我們脫了鞋襪，摺起褲腳，在海邊流連一番。 
### FROM WEST TO EAST
在 Eugene 住了四天後便坐巴士去Seattle，這是我第一次坐長途巴士  (Trailways 或 Greyhound)，  美國巴士的速度很快，隨時有七八十咪  ，可和大貨櫃車比美。那些大貨櫃車可說是高速公路的殺星，前後共有十八個輪，普通的私家車若與這些殺星相撞， 必散無疑。  
Seattle是一個美麗的城市，有著  名的 Space Needle 及 Monorail  ，都是六零年代博覽會的遣物，附近有  很多名山大川，Mt. Rainier有一萬  四千多呎高，在Downtown也可看  到它積雪的山頂，非常壯觀，我曾到過  山脚的 Paradise（海拔五千四百呎）  
，那麼終年積雪。在雪地上步行雖然是  危险，但另有一番滋味，沿着Paradise  
的小徑，我往上爬了数百呎，直至我到  一條冰河的側面，四周都充满了雪，当我漸漸發覺我的面及耳朵開始凍得沒有  感覺，我便忽忽下山。我在離開 Sale 前到過Mt.St. Helen 的災區，參觀了  一些被火山灰埋藏的房屋及被溶岩破壊的公路及橋樑。 
Houston在美國的南部，可算是  一個非常富有的城市，我到Houston  時已是晚上十時牛，找不到價錢適中的酒店，结果在Hyatt Regency 的  Lobby坐到牛夜二時，再轉在一些  Underground Shopping Mall System 的 Corridor 中睡覺， 早上我  到公園中睡覺，結果兩個警察叫醒，我在市中心區遊蕩，然後坐巴士去看  Houston Medical Centre 及 Astrodome 在巴士站等待巴士時，突然有  一個黑種傳教士大嚷着，要人悔改，跟  随上帝「Those Who Repent Are The Children of God, Those Who Don't Are Bastards ， 大講道理，巴士來了，每一個人都趕着上車， 那教士也越叫越大聲，最後巴士開動時，他大叫是上帝命令巴士開動。晚上我  回到機場睡覺，又Underground  
Shuttle Subway 到各個Terminals 遊荡。  
我在美國的交通工具大部份是飛機，在香港可以買到兩個月有效的多程機票，價錢在三千餘元左右，可停十一處地方。我跟着的一程是去 Rochestor，我在那里的朋友租了一部「Rent A  Wreck (Chrysler的Monte Carlo)，這部車可算是「Wreck」，在高速  
公路上我們險些送了命，當時我们的車  速是五十五咪，車頭蓋突然掀開了，完  全遮蔽了擋風玻璃，我們很幸運，當時高速公路上只有很少的車輛行駛，否則效果便會不堪設想。  
我和他結果换了車，到Corning 參觀玻璃廠，整個市就是一個很大的製造玻璃場，有介紹玻璃的歷史及科學，館也有人示範做玻璃器皿·接着我們又到  Niagara Falls 觀赏瀑布，遥望着流水感嘆一番·Niagara Falls 不是那麽美麗，It is Not Very Imposing  
after all。  
### BOSTON-LOBSTER
離開了Rochestor，我繼續向東岸出發，來到一個頗有傳統及氣派的城市——Boston，一個從香港移民美國的家庭接待我，Boston的海鲜很出名，第一晚已經吃到險些兒大瀉，Clams，Cherry Stones, Oysters, Crabs 源源不絕入口，還有清蒸龍蝦，好味好 味！ Boston可说是美國最有Culture  的城市之一，有較重的歐陸感覺，不像西岸城市那般新奇和友善。這里的猶太人有很大的势力，有很多猶太人的企業、學校及商店。Boston也是東岸的教育中心，著名的 Harvard University，MIT, Boston University 等都在那里 ，校園雖然沒有西岸的大學那麼美麗但  學術風氣很重，Harvard Square是  大學生文化的集中地，有各類的商店，還有在街頭擺賣的小販。在 Boston Downtown，有很多美丽宏偉的建築物，例如 Christian Science Church 的總部，Hall of Justice 等 ，Boston 的大會堂及附近的 Boston Common（是一连串的購物中心）時常都有露天的表演，這些地方都是游客的好去處。Boston的地鐵也值得一坐，因為這是全美最古老的地鐵系統。 
### NEW YORK  
New York是一個多姿多彩的大城市，它有聯合國總部、世界上最大的自然博物馆(American Museum of  Natural History）華爾街（Wall  St.)、World Trade Centre、  
Statue of Liberty，著名的Broadway、Radio City、Harlem……。 在Broadway、Times Square 及 42th Street 附近，有很多著名舞台刻  的演出·我在Edison Theatre 看過  
了Oh！Calcutta！這些舞台劇大都上演了一段很長的時間。這一區可說得 是 NewYork的文化及藝術的集中地——無論是 Cultivated 或 Vulgar 的  這區也是警察雲集的方，因為 New York 實在是太混亂，沒有人可以担保你可以招搖過市。  
### WASHINGTON D.C.  
聽說各國的間諜都雲集首都。但這  地方卻給人一種與世無爭的感覺，我很難想像得到影響整個世界的決策會在這些地方進行，Washington D.C.實在太寧静了。在這里的遊客可以進入Congress Building, Congress Library，White Palace 及其它有府大樓參觀，WashingtonC.D. 還有很多著名的 Monuments 及 Memorial Halls Smithsonian Institute的展  覽館都集中在這些建築物附近。  
## 大學生活  
我從Washington D.C.返回 Chicago，在Chicago 附近的一個大學城 (Illinois State University at Normal）住了兩星期，體驗中國留學生的生活，我在西岸曾到過UCLA，UC Berkeley, Stanford University, Whittier College 及 University of Oregon，Eugene，這些學都有很美麗的校園及先進的設備，每一間校園都有特色，UCBerkeley是六十年代學運的發源地，有很多不同生活方式的學生，也有很多古靈精怪的團體例如 什麼League of Gays and Lesbians 等，雖然Berkeley 已經没有六七十年代時候那麼激進化，但仍然有很多校園政治性的示威及抗議行動，我離開 San Francisco 那天便有一枚炸彈在校園中爆炸。  
差不多所有大學的學生會都提供多元化的服務，包括旅遊、膳食、買賣書本、日用品及衣服等。  
我在Normal 住在 International House，，和各國的留學生一起，香港的學生大都很勤力，除了讀書外，還在學校工作，他们大多是在Cafeteria 做牛職，我也在 dishroom做過  scrubber（正牌洗大饼）及 cart  washer，Scrubber 的工作十分繁重，  通常要在兩小时内洗完數千隻碗碟，整 條Iine有六七個 Scrubber，而大部份的工作是集中在一小時中，頗為辛苦·很多香港學生都担任沒有人喜歡（他們都沒有工作證，所以要做On-Campus Jobs) 工作，美國人的大學生卻很喜歡在Off-Campus 做 Part-Time  
，因為待遇較好，而工作的種類也很多 McDonald, Burger King, Pizza  Hut 等都會請本土的學生，很多私人機構也僱用他們。 
留學生的生活通常很苦悶，距離自  己的家鄉太遠，而且不能適應美國的文化，我不甚贊成不成熟的人到外國留學  ，因為自己的所以缺點在這些情况下會表露無遺，要看清楚一個人很容易，只要和他相處數天，便可以感覺得到。留學生對男女關係也看得很隨便，很多留學生都說：「有女不要送她到美國。」
中共及台灣特務在校園中很活躍， 聞說他們每個月都有一筆錢來搞一些政  治活動，中國同學會內也有政治派系鬥爭。事實上，有些大學有兩三個中國同學·在Normal校園內，我從香港學生方面知道有一個台灣特務定期接受疑項，利用中國同學會的名義搞一些反共的宣傳及刊物。 
### CHINATOWN  
我比较喜歡 San Francisco的唐人街，這里的氣氛很親切，街道頗窄及斜，有點像中環的威靈頓街一帶，有很多凌亂的招牌及店舖，差不多每一個人都講唐話。超級市場有我喜歡的維他奶、蝦子麵。戲院有「最佳拍檔」、「歡樂神仙窩」等港產電影。也有很多港產的唱片及電視劇的錄影帶夜靜時還有  食店賣雲吞面（雖然是五美元美金一碗  
）。  
New York的唐人街和SanFrancisco的相似，只是地方更污穢、更凌亂，整個Chinatown像個大街市，在香港買到的東西，這里也買到，這裏像上環區的翻版，建築物雖然頗舊， 但不失有點「香港味」。  
相比來说，Seattle的唐人街太舊  ，但也较neat，不像香港的街道，而 LA的唐人街較大，建築物也較新，也  失去了香港那種「擠逼」的滋味。  
### AMERICA IS  
America is a place where  
anything can happen a place  
abounding with contradictions,  
adventures and opportunities
很多美國人極度浪費資源及食物，我做了 Scrubber數天，時常看着一碟碟沒有  吃過的食物或一杯杯沒有飲過的牛奶倒入污水或垃圾槽中，心中也有點難過。  
美國人太喜歡表演及表現自我，他們的善意及態度大都流於表面化，他们的文  化沒有一種較深的體驗，可能是這一代的美國人沒有受過苦痛，可能是精神價  值的崩潰，使這一代的美國人無所適從，思想混亂。  
### 後記 
回到香港，已经覺得香港很陌生，我落機的第一個感覺是到了一個頗落後的東南亞城市。我只是離開了個半月，感覺便變得那麼的快·是不是香港變得太快？或是我變得太快？可能两者俱是，我不知道。

### Travels in America
**By Big Head B**
Finally made it to America! All the beef jerky, dried shrimp, and Great Wall brand canned pork I “smuggled” cleared customs without a hitch. The elderly couple traveling with me weren't so lucky; all the dried pork and beef jerky they brought were confiscated. Going through customs in Hawaii requires you to be very slick, because the customs officials there are quite slick themselves—they actually understand and speak Chinese, but when you're passing through, they play dumb and wait patiently for you to slip up so they can confiscate your treasures.
#### Los Angeles
After another few hours of flying, I arrived in the West Coast’s largest city, Los Angeles. My first impression of America was that most of the houses are very low-rise; the high-rise skyscrapers are all concentrated in Down-Town. In Los Angeles, all I saw were crisscrossing roads and overpasses—even an American who has lived there for decades could easily get lost. Because LA is so massive and public transit isn't very convenient, cars are basically a necessity. The sheer number of vehicles is enormous, and rush-hour traffic jams are terrible. During my few days in LA, I stayed at the homes of two Hong Kong friends living in the US and an American couple.
My friends are a brother and sister. The older brother works in LA, while the younger sister studies at Whittier College (where Nixon also went to school). Their lives are very simple and plain, almost a bit boring. There, I met an exchange student from Mainland China. He was in his early 40s, had already graduated from a university back home, and came to the US to earn a bachelor’s degree in English. He and I talked about the Cultural Revolution and the democracy movement; he had completely lost faith in politics and just wanted three square meals a day and peace for his family. Being able to have that was enough to make him content.
While in LA, I toured Down-Town. The livelier area is Broadway, which has plenty of shops and movie theaters—a bit like Mong Kok in Hong Kong. Here, you can see people from all walks of life and with different lifestyles. I could also feel that Black, White, and Mexican people each have distinct cultures. The way Black people walk almost looks like dancing; some even carry around a radio boombox, singing and dancing along. When they talk to you, their slang, pronunciation, and intonation can leave you completely baffled. In front of LA City Hall, there is a bronze statue of John Lennon, and people often lay flowers before it. Besides City Hall, the LA Civic Center also has a good number of massive buildings. Not far from the Civic Center are Little Tokyo and Chinatown, where Japanese and Chinese people concentrate and reside, respectively. Both places have a distinct flavor. Chinatown's streets are quite narrow and the buildings are pretty low-rise, with plenty of eateries, videotape and AV shops, grocery stores, and banks lining the roads.
**Strange News in America** Believe it or not, America actually has local governments with socialist tendencies! In a county here (called Santa Monica), a group of radical socialists won the election. They address each other as "Comrade," renamed the place the "Peoples' Republic of Santa Monica," and pushed through a series of social reforms, such as regulating the activities and development of big corporations in the area. When interviewed on TV, they admitted to implementing socialist policies, yet the federal and state governments didn't seem to exert pressure to change them. It was hard for me to imagine the American government allowing such things to exist.
**American Family Life** In LA, I stayed at the home of an elderly couple. The husband is a retired Air Force Colonel who now works as a Contract Manager at a famous space and aeronautical engineering firm. During WWII, he was stationed around Sichuan and Guilin, flying B-19 bombers. He loves Chinese people very much because when his plane was shot down during a mission, he relied on the help of Chinese locals to make it back to his base from enemy-controlled territory within a few weeks. He holds many precious memories—Flying Tigers members, the scenery of Guilin—and has kept many old photos.
Staying with him, I could feel that Americans have a deep respect for the individual. He was very attentive to other people's feelings and needs, but would never pry into someone's past life or background. Other details also reflected his deep respect for privacy: I stayed in the guest room on the lower level of his house, and he would never casually enter the room to clean up. His own bedroom was upstairs, and he didn't invite me up to look around. He once said: _"Maturity is knowing how to live with unresolved conflicts."_ He is 62 this year, yet he is still taking courses in personnel management at the UCLA Extension Center and taking exams. I don't know how deeply war affected him; he was also involved in planning work during the Vietnam War. He is a military man, yet he doesn't have the temperament or attitude I imagined a soldier would have. In his family life, he shares all the household chores; seeing his relationship with his wife, I knew he wasn't a male chauvinist at all.
Most elderly people in America love pets, and they are no exception. Their children aren't around, so with no other emotional outlet, they keep a few dogs and treat them just like their own kids. The dogs are an integral part of this couple's life. Perhaps the world is just unfair this way: the room and board of these pets are better than those of many Black and Mexican people.
#### Arizona
I stayed in Phoenix, Arizona, for five days and joined a few local tours to visit the Grand Canyon and Tucson. The Grand Canyon is one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Standing on the rim of the canyon, you can see the river channel over 7,000 feet below, as well as the opposite rim several miles away. Due to the sunlight and the shadows cast by clouds, the layers of sedimentary rock in the Grand Canyon exhibit several unique colors. The grandeur of this canyon makes one feel tiny in the face of nature—it can even evoke a sense of fear. The Grand Canyon is like a solemn, sacred palace quietly evolving through history.
Tucson has a strong Western feel, but the most unforgettable thing is the cacti. On the way to Old Town Tucson, I could see countless cacti dozens of feet tall, standing like green giants in the vast desert. Old Town Tucson is a movie set previously used for shooting Western films, but it has now been turned into a tourist center. Every day there are sheriff-versus-bandit gunfights staged there, alongside many buildings mimicking an 18th/19th-century Western town. There is also a Chinatown here; back then, most Chinese were miners or railroad workers, though some made a living running laundromats. Near Tucson, the St. Xavier Mission is a historic church with a rich Spanish style. In these places, I found myself imagining that I was a pioneer of the Old West, exploring everywhere and discovering novel, exciting things. At the Desert Zoo in Tucson, they keep many live spiders, scorpions, centipedes, snakes, and other desert animals. Seeing them reminded me of what my friend once said: "Life in Arizona isn't easy—the temperatures are too high, and lethal Black Widows pop up in your house all the time!" As a result, he moved from Mesa, Arizona, to Sunnyvale, California.
During my time in Phoenix, I stayed at the YMCA. I vaguely remember that it was there I smelled marijuana for the first time—whiffs of a pungent, burning odor. Temperatures in Phoenix are very high (around 110°F) with low humidity, making it easy to get heatstroke. On Saturdays and Sundays, the entire city of Phoenix feels like a ghost town; very few people roam the streets, most shops are closed, and public buses stop running. Most of those wandering the streets are drunks, Black people, and Mexican people, many of whom are extremely poor. Several times while buying food at the supermarket to fill my stomach, I witnessed embarrassing situations where Black shoppers didn't have enough money for groceries. They usually tried to stretch their money to buy as much as possible—for instance, if they had $7.20, they’d try to buy $7.30 worth of goods, hoping the cashier wouldn't mind. They were rarely successful, after which they'd argue with the cashier to play a stalling game. When the cashier held firm and they knew their trick wouldn't work, they'd give up one of the items.
I also remember one night when a French tourist and I were walking back to the YMCA and met a young Black man. Holding a small plaque, he asked us about the words engraved on it—he couldn't read. (The plaque read _God Grant You Serenity_). I read it out loud to him, but he didn't understand the meanings of "Grant" or "Serenity." The fate of Mexican people is also quite tragic; most are undocumented immigrants with meager incomes. In Phoenix, I visited some impoverished neighborhoods. Although the living conditions weren't as bad as Hong Kong's slums, most houses were dilapidated, with backyards piled high with broken furniture and junk cars.
The French tourist of Polish descent I met in Phoenix was a quintessential Frenchman—he sported a stylish handlebar mustache, was very romantic, and loved wandering the world. Although he was already a 32-year-old high school teacher, he still retained a sense of "childlike innocence." When he and I were touring near the State Capitol, the automatic sprinkler system happened to turn on to water the surrounding lawns and plants. He immediately kicked off his shoes, ran onto the grass to play in the water, and shouted, _"Oh! Yo! Yo! Yo!"_
Over our short two or three days together, I learned a lot about America's European cultural roots. My French friend had traveled through most of Continental Europe and visited America nine times. What impressed me most was his experience traveling back to Poland. Many absurd things happened there: for example, hotel rates were divided into three tiers. The most expensive was for tourists from capitalist countries, followed by tourists from friendly nations (including Polish citizens themselves), while the most discounted rates were reserved for Soviets.
#### SAN FRANCISCO
San Francisco is a strange yet distinctive city with all kinds of people—gays and lesbians, tourists, drug pushers, radicals, all kinds of religious fanatics. It’s a real mixed bag of dragons and snakes, yet San Francisco gives off a cheerful, relaxed, and friendly vibe. The Golden Gate Bridge, Fisherman's Wharf, and Golden Gate Park are all great spots to visit, not to mention the Cable Cars, Chinatown, and All Kinds of Entertainment (You Know What I Mean!).
The adult industry in San Francisco is very developed, with plenty of XXX-Rated Movies and live shows. These live shows are live shows in the truest sense, as the performers might invite customers on stage to give a live, unscripted demonstration with them. Even the X-rated movies alone feature many daring scenes—anything you can imagine can be seen on screen. But after watching these X-rated movies for 15 or 20 minutes, they lose their appeal. There's no mystery left whatsoever, and watching too much actually makes you feel sick to your stomach.
**Hong Kong Students in America** I have a friend living in Sunnyvale who is studying Engineering at Stanford while working at a large electronics factory. His income is quite respectable at around $2,000 USD a month. His apartment has 400–500 sq ft of usable space, and the rent is about $400. His life in America is rather dull; during holidays, his only option is to go camping or traveling to National Parks with friends. He and I traveled to Kings Canyon and Sequoia National Park, where we saw huge pine trees and the world's largest tree (the General Sherman Tree). These pines take on a striking red color under the sunlight, and some have very peculiar shapes. The pinecones are massive—some 8 to 10 inches long and 2 to 3 inches in diameter.
In Oregon, I also visited a friend pursuing his Ph.D. at the University of Oregon in Eugene. He works as a TA at the university and lives a relaxed life. He and I visited Florence, a small coastal town. There is a sand dune there that stretches over 40 miles long and 2 to 3 miles wide. To get to the ocean, you have to cross this desert-like sand dune. We decided to try walking across this "desert" ourselves, and it ended up taking us nearly two hours to reach the shore. There was hardly anyone there; wisps of fog swept across the beach, scattered by the cool sea breeze. The ocean water was freezing, with only a few flocks of seabirds wading near the edge. We took off our shoes and socks, rolled up our pant legs, and lingered by the sea for a while.
#### FROM WEST TO EAST
After staying in Eugene for four days, I took a bus to Seattle. This was my first time taking a long-distance bus (Trailways or Greyhound). American buses drive very fast, often hitting 70 or 80 mph, rivaling large semi-trucks. Those big rigs are absolute menaces on the highway; with 18 wheels in total, a regular sedan colliding with one would be smashed to pieces.
Seattle is a beautiful city. The famous Space Needle and Monorail are both relics of the 1960s World's Fair. Surrounding the city are famous mountains and rivers; Mt. Rainier stands at over 14,000 feet, and its snow-capped peak can be seen right from Downtown—a truly magnificent sight. I visited Paradise at the foot of the mountain (5,400 feet above sea level), where snow remains year-round. Walking on the snow was dangerous, but it had a unique charm. Following the trail at Paradise, I climbed up a few hundred feet until I reached the side of a glacier, surrounded by snow. When I gradually realized my face and ears were going numb from the cold, I hurried back down the mountain. Before leaving Seattle, I visited the Mt. St. Helens disaster zone and saw houses buried in volcanic ash, as well as highways and bridges destroyed by lava.
Houston is in the American South and can be considered a very wealthy city. When I arrived in Houston, it was already 10:30 PM, and I couldn't find a reasonably priced hotel. In the end, I sat in the lobby of the Hyatt Regency until 2:00 AM, then moved to sleep in the corridor of an underground shopping mall system. In the morning, I went to sleep in a park, only to be woken up by two police officers. I wandered around the downtown area, then caught a bus to see the Houston Medical Center and the Astrodome. While waiting at the bus stop, a Black preacher suddenly started shouting at the top of his lungs, calling on people to repent and follow God: _"Those Who Repent Are The Children of God, Those Who Don't Are Bastards!"_ He preached loudly, and when the bus arrived, everyone rushed to board. The preacher yelled louder and louder, and finally, as the bus pulled away, he roared that it was God who had commanded the bus to depart. That night, I went back to the airport to sleep, riding the Underground Shuttle Subway between terminals just to wander around.
My primary mode of transportation in America was flying. In Hong Kong, you can buy a multi-stop ticket valid for two months for around $3,000 HKD, allowing up to 11 layovers. My next stop was Rochester. A friend of mine there rented a car from "Rent-A-Wreck" (a Chrysler Monte Carlo). That car truly lived up to being a "wreck"—we nearly lost our lives on the highway! We were traveling at 55 mph when the hood suddenly popped open, completely blocking the windshield. We were very lucky that traffic on the highway was sparse at that moment; otherwise, the consequences would have been unimaginable.
My friend and I eventually swapped cars and went to Corning to visit the glass factory. The whole city is like one giant glass manufacturing plant, featuring exhibitions on the history and science of glass, as well as live glassblowing demonstrations. Next, we headed to Niagara Falls to take in the sight, gazing at the rushing water with a sense of awe. Yet Niagara Falls wasn't all that breathtaking—_It is Not Very Imposing after all_.
#### BOSTON—LOBSTER
Leaving Rochester, I continued heading toward the East Coast and arrived in a city rich in tradition and grandeur—Boston. I was hosted by a family who had immigrated to the US from Hong Kong. Boston's seafood is famous; on the very first night, I ate so much I nearly ended up with severe diarrhea. Clams, cherrystones, oysters, and crabs flowed endlessly into my mouth, along with steamed lobster—so delicious, so delicious!
Boston can be called one of America's most cultured cities, carrying a stronger European feel and lacking the novelty and easy friendliness of West Coast cities. Jewish people hold significant influence here, with many Jewish enterprises, schools, and shops. Boston is also the educational hub of the East Coast, home to famous institutions like Harvard University, MIT, and Boston University. Although the campuses aren't as expansive as those on the West Coast, the academic atmosphere is dense. Harvard Square is a central hub for student culture, packed with all kinds of shops and street vendors. In Downtown Boston, there are many beautiful, grand buildings, such as the Christian Science Church headquarters and the Hall of Justice. Boston City Hall and nearby Boston Common (which connects to a series of shopping areas) frequently host outdoor performances, making them great spots for tourists. Boston's subway is also worth a ride, as it is the oldest subway system in the United States.
#### NEW YORK
New York is a colorful, multifaceted metropolis. It houses the UN Headquarters, the world's largest natural history museum (the American Museum of Natural History), Wall Street, the World Trade Center, the Statue of Liberty, the famous Broadway, Radio City, Harlem... Near Broadway, Times Square, and 42nd Street, there are many famous stage productions. I saw _Oh! Calcutta!_ at the Edison Theatre; most of these plays have been running for a very long time. This area can be called New York's hub for culture and art—whether cultivated or vulgar. It is also an area heavily patrolled by police because New York is simply too chaotic; no one can guarantee you'll make it across town unscathed if you flaunt yourself.
#### WASHINGTON D.C.
Word has it that spies from every nation gather in the capital. Yet the place gave off a peaceful vibe, detached from worldly conflicts. It was hard for me to imagine that decisions impacting the entire world are made here—Washington D.C. is simply too quiet. Tourists here can enter the Capitol Building, the Library of Congress, the White House, and other government buildings for tours. Washington D.C. also features many famous monuments and memorial halls; the exhibition halls of the Smithsonian Institution are concentrated around these structures.
#### University Life
From Washington D.C., I returned to Chicago and stayed for two weeks in a college town near Chicago (Illinois State University at Normal) to experience the life of Chinese international students. On the West Coast, I had visited UCLA, UC Berkeley, Stanford University, Whittier College, and the University of Oregon in Eugene. All these universities have beautiful campuses and advanced facilities, each with its own character. UC Berkeley was the birthplace of the 1960s student movement and has a wide variety of student lifestyles, along with all sorts of weird organizations like the League of Gays and Lesbians. Although Berkeley isn't as radicalized as it was in the '60s and '70s, political demonstrations and protests still frequently take place on campus. On the day I left San Francisco, a bomb exploded on campus.
Almost all university student unions offer a wide range of services, including travel bookings, dining, book buying/selling, daily necessities, and clothing.
At Normal, I stayed at the International House alongside international students from various countries. Hong Kong students were generally very hardworking; besides studying, they worked on campus, mostly doing part-time jobs in the cafeteria. I worked in the dishroom as a scrubber (a genuine dish-washer!) and a cart washer. The scrubber's work was extremely heavy: usually, several thousand dishes had to be washed within two hours. There were 6 or 7 scrubbers along the entire line, and most of the work was packed into a single hour, making it quite exhausting. Many Hong Kong students took on jobs that no one else wanted (since they didn't have off-campus work permits, they had to settle for on-campus jobs). American students preferred working off-campus part-time because the pay was better and the variety was greater—McDonald's, Burger King, Pizza Hut, and various private businesses were all eager to hire local students.
The life of an international student is usually quite lonely—being so far from home and unable to fully adapt to American culture. I don't particularly advocate sending immature people abroad to study, as all of one's flaws are exposed under these circumstances. It's easy to see right through a person: just spend a few days with them, and you'll get a full sense of who they are. International students also tend to hold casual attitudes toward romantic relationships; many international students say, "If you have a girlfriend, don't send her to America."
CCP and Taiwanese operatives are very active on campus. Word has it that they receive a monthly stipend to organize political activities, leading to political factionalism even within the Chinese Students Association. In fact, some universities have two or three competing Chinese student groups. On the Normal campus, I learned from Hong Kong students that a Taiwanese operative regularly received funding to produce anti-communist propaganda and publications under the guise of the Chinese Students Association.
#### CHINATOWN
I personally prefer San Francisco's Chinatown. The atmosphere here feels warm and familiar; the streets are rather narrow and steep, reminiscent of Wellington Street in Central, Hong Kong. It's packed with messy shop signs and storefronts, and almost everyone speaks Cantonese. The supermarkets carry items I love, like Vita Soy and shrimp-egg noodles. The cinemas screen Hong Kong films like _Aces Go Places_ and _Heaven Can Help_. There are also plenty of Hong Kong record releases and TV drama videotapes. Late at night, eateries even sell wonton noodles (even if it's $5 USD a bowl!).
New York's Chinatown is similar to San Francisco's, except it's dirtier and messier. The whole Chinatown feels like a massive wet market—anything you can buy in Hong Kong, you can buy here. It's like a carbon copy of the Sheung Wan district: the buildings are quite old, but it retains a real "Hong Kong flavor."
By comparison, Seattle's Chinatown is too old, though neater and less like Hong Kong's streets. LA's Chinatown is larger with newer buildings, but it lacks that crowded, bustling Hong Kong vibe.
#### AMERICA IS...
_America is a place where anything can happen—a place abounding with contradictions, adventures, and opportunities._
Many Americans are extremely wasteful with resources and food. After working as a scrubber for a few days, seeing plate after plate of untouched food or full glasses of milk poured down the drain or into trash chutes made me feel genuinely sad.
Americans love to put on a show and express themselves; their goodwill and attitudes often feel superficial. Their culture lacks a deeper sense of lived experience—perhaps because this generation of Americans hasn't known true hardship, or perhaps because the collapse of spiritual values has left them directionless and confused.
#### Epilogue
Returning to Hong Kong, the city already felt strange to me. My very first impression stepping off the plane was that I had arrived in a rather backward Southeast Asian city. I had only been gone for a month and a half, yet my perceptions shifted so quickly. Is Hong Kong changing too fast? Or am I the one who changed too fast? Maybe it's both; I don't know.
